01 · The idea

A month, not a prompt.

Most "make reels with AI" posts show one prompt and one result. The promise here is bigger: one sentence plans a whole month. So the reel has to answer the obvious doubt ("won't they all be the same random AI reels?") by showing the order the work happens in, like an agency would do it: research first, then the brand, then the scripts, then the reels.

The structure follows that. A deck of reel cards rolls to 30 on frame 0, the sentence is typed in a small chat card, six identical "generic AI reels" get crossed out, and a row of four desks (Research, Brand, Script, Reel) carries the middle. The proof at the end is a calendar filled with frames of reels we actually made. Catalina, the Lab's character, presents from the corner.

02 · References

What Claude needed before the first prompt.

This is the Lab's own piece, so the brand is ours. A reel on the same topic gave us the order of the ideas; the look, the script and every prop were made from scratch for this one.

A tracker that carries the middle

Four numbered desks appear on "agency" and stay: one lights up per step and gets a check when it's done (1/4 → 4/4). The viewer always knows where they are in the process.

A colour per block

Every block floods the frame with a new colour from its focus, alternating light and dark: cream, clay, navy, deep green, amber, ink, cream, navy. The step changes before you read it.

Chunky cards, hard shadows

Thick ink outlines and a solid offset shadow, no blur. Loud, graphic and readable on a phone after Instagram compresses it.

Real proof

The calendar is filled with frames from reels we actually made, not mock thumbnails. If the claim is "a month of reels", the last frame has to show a month of real ones.

Palette

The Lab's colours carry the frame; the step blocks add full-intensity colour so each one reads at a glance.

#F6F0E6 cream#D97757 clay#141A2E navy#1F4D3A green#F2C14E amber
Presenter

Catalina, from her real images only: three short image-to-video clips (wave, think-then-point, wink) and full-body poses from her character sheet in between, swapped in place.

03 · One-time setup

Before the prompt.

Step 01

Install Claude Code.

Follow the official guide at docs.claude.com (Claude Code overview) for your system, then open it inside an empty project folder.

Step 02

Node 22+ and FFmpeg.

The scenes are plain JavaScript drawing on an HTML canvas. Node runs a headless browser that renders each frame, and FFmpeg joins the frames and the audio into the MP4.

Step 03

Python 3.10+.

For the audio and the presenter layer: mixing the voice with the sound effects, checking loudness and compositing the presenter's cut-outs frame by frame.

Step 04

An ElevenLabs API key.

Put it in a .env file in the project and ask Claude to request word-level timestamps with the audio. Those timestamps are what every cue reads.

Optional

A style guide for Claude.

A short Markdown file with your palette, fonts, pacing and safe zone, which Claude reads before writing any scene. We used a paid motion-design guide; your own notes work too.

04 · Claude session

One brief, a test, then the checks.

Below is the master prompt you can paste, followed by the two quality-control messages: the stills review and the final render.

00:01 · master prompt · claude code
Make a 35-second vertical edu reel for The AI Editing Lab, 1080x1920 at 30 fps, all in English. Topic: planning a month of reels for a brand with one sentence to Claude.

1. Script. Hook in under 2 seconds: "Thirty reels for your brand, and it all starts with one sentence to Claude." Then the sentence itself ("Plan thirty reels for my brand."), the objection ("Random AI reels? No. It works like an agency."), the four steps in order (research: competitors, what works in the niche, how the brand looks and sounds; scripts written from that research, not from a template; each script becomes a real reel with voice, motion and captions), and the payoff: thirty days, one calendar, all filled. Close with: "Comment MONTH and we'll send you the workflow."

2. Voice. ElevenLabs, voice "Jessica", natural speed (1.0). Save every word's start and end to words.json; every cue reads a word time, never a guessed second.

3. Metaphor. A month of reels as a deck of cards and a wall calendar. The "agency" is a row of four desks (Research, Brand, Script, Reel) that stays on screen as a tracker from the objection to the reel, one desk lit per step and a check when it's done.

4. Look. Everything drawn in code on an HTML canvas: chunky cards with a thick ink outline and a hard offset shadow, mono "// labels", an orange Claude spark. Every block floods a new full-frame colour from its focus, alternating light and dark: cream, clay, navy, deep green, amber, ink, cream, navy. Orange only on the focus of the moment. The prompt in the chat card is small, like a real chat, typed letter by letter on the words.

5. Honesty. No real competitor names or logos (@competitor_a/b/c), no invented numbers ("outlier" and "trending" are UI labels). The calendar fills with frames of our own real reels.

6. Layout. Everything important inside x 90-990 and above y 1400; keep the bottom-right corner (x > 650, y > 1045) empty for our presenter.

7. Process. Build a 10-second test of the first three blocks first. Then the rest in parallel, sharing one kit. Show me a stills sheet and the motion and originality checks before the final render.

What came back: the script, a block-by-block storyboard, the ElevenLabs narration with 96 time-stamped words, a shared kit (colour floods, cards, the four-desk tracker) and a 10-second test of the first three blocks. After the test was approved, two builders worked in parallel on the rest, both reading the same word clock.

00:02 · stills before render · claude code
Before the final render, export a stills sheet: one frame every 1.5 seconds from frame 0. Check every block for: something changing on every stressed word, nothing frozen longer than a second, the block full at its cut, text readable on a phone, the colour change landing on the cut, the presenter's corner empty, and nothing that promises a service. Fix everything in one pass and show me the sheet again.
00:03 · final render · claude code
Approved. Composite our presenter Catalina on top from her real images: a waving clip at the start, a "thinks, then points at you" clip on the objection, full-body poses from her character sheet in between (swapped in place every ~3 s with a short crossfade), and a wink clip on the last word. Render 1080x1920 at 30 fps, 14 Mbps, the mix at -14 LUFS, and make the cover inside y 300-1480.

What came back: 35.1 seconds at 1080×1920 and 30 fps, 14 Mbps, voice plus 48 sound effects placed on real events, and the cover.

05 · What Claude built

Four desks, one month.

HOOK

The deck rolls to 30

A fan of nine playing reel cards, a counter rolling 01 → 30 from frame 0, a "YOUR BRAND" tag that swings in, and a one-line strip that the whole deck squashes toward on "one sentence".

PROMPT

Small, like a real chat

The strip becomes a Claude chat card; the prompt types at chat size following the words, "30" gets underlined, and on "brand" the send button turns it into a sent bubble.

THE DOUBT

Six identical clones

Six grey "TOP 5 TIPS" cards deal in, all with the same "AI" sticker and glitching in sync, next to a "same template ×6" card. A big orange X slams across them on "No."

RESEARCH

A lens that moves to the focus

A magnifier flies out of desk 1 and glides to each focus: three competitor cards with playing mini reels (one marked "outlier"), a niche chart with two bars shooting up, a brand kit with swatches, "Aa" and a live waveform.

SCRIPTS

From research, not a template

The research packs into a folder that feeds arrows into a stack of scripts (×30); HOOK, 0:03 and CTA lines type in, and a grey "TEMPLATE" card tears in two.

REEL

The card becomes a phone

A script card unfolds into a playing phone while a layers panel stacks voice, motion and captions one by one, each pushed in on its word. The tracker ends at 4/4.

PROOF

Thirty real frames

A wall calendar drops in on its pin, a deck is dealt into the 30 cells in a diagonal wave, each card turning into a frame of one of our real reels, and the counter lands on 30/30.

LEVEL UP

Test, then build in parallel

One builder made the shared kit and the first three blocks as a 10-second test. Once approved, two builders made the rest at the same time, passing a hand-off (where the script card and the tracker sit) so the blocks join without seams.

07 · Decisions

Where the taste is.

01

Answer the doubt early

"Random AI reels?" is what the viewer is already thinking at second 7. Saying it out loud, and crossing it out, buys the rest of the reel.

02

Plan is the honest verb

One sentence plans the month; each reel is then made from its script. The prompt says "Plan", not "Make", because that's what actually happens.

03

One tracker for the middle

Four desks that stay on screen turn a list of steps into progress the eye can follow.

04

Every cue is a word

The X lands on "No.", the lens on "competitors", the tear on "template", the 30th cell on "filled".

05

Proof over promise

The calendar shows our own reels. No mock thumbnails, no invented numbers, no real competitor names.

06

A corner for the presenter

The bottom-right stays empty in every scene, so Catalina never covers a card and the cards never cover her.

08 · Watch out

What went wrong, and the fix.

"Make 30 reels" overpromises

One sentence doesn't render thirty finished reels. The fix: the prompt plans the month, and the reel shows each script becoming a reel.

A sample CTA that competes

The demo script card first ended with another "Comment ___" keyword, which fought with MONTH. The fix: a neutral line ("Save this for later.").

Flat stretches

The motion check flagged still moments in the hook and the prompt. The fix: a slow sunburst behind the deck, rings from the cursor, cards that keep swaying.

A presenter clip that drifts from the voice

The "think, then point" clip only works if the point lands on "No." The fix: start the clip so its thinking part covers the question and the point hits the answer.

09 · Ship it

From render to post.

Step 01

Export at a real bitrate.

Thin mono labels and calendar thumbnails don't survive low bitrates. Encode at 12–16 Mbps.

Step 02

Check the loudness.

Aim for −14 LUFS with a true peak at or below −1.5 dB, voice above the sound effects.

Step 03

Make the cover.

The profile grid crops covers to 3:4, so keep the title and the main image between y 300 and 1480.

Step 04

Caption with the credits.

Say what was made and how, give the comment keyword, and credit the voice. On ElevenLabs' free plan, credit it as "Voice: ElevenLabs".

ffmpeg -i final.mp4 -af ebur128=peak=true -f null -

My version is about [my topic], for [my audience], in [duration].
